The spouse of pianist and composer [Anton] Halm wished for a ringlet of Beethoven's hair. She approached Karl Holz to act as intermediary. On his plea the master granted permission to send his great admiress a tuft of hair from a billy goat's beard, as its grey and strong hair could well be compared to his own.

The dame, overjoyed with this relic of her patron saint of the arts, boasted that present far and wide. But soon, she found out what trick Beethoven had played on her. Her husband, who was still deeply saturated with the point d'honneur of an army officer, reported what they had heard in a tetchy letter to the master. He, recognizing the inflicted insult, remedied the incident by cutting himself a ringlet of his own hair and sending it directly to the dame, enclosed in a card requesting forgiveness.

This incident happened in 1826.

Source:

Schindler, Anton: Anton Schindler's Beethoven-Biographie: Neudruck herausgegeben von Dr. Alfred Christian Kalischer, Verlag Schuster & LÃ¶ffler (1909) p.536f (available at the Internet Archive in original German)

My partner and I just started a company, so we're utilizing some temp space in a suburban office park. We both hate the suburbs, but it was affordable and we service a large client nearby so it makes sense in the short term. We'll eventually buy space downtown.

Right down the hall from us is a company that is constantly interviewing candidates. It's a revolving door, and at times there are a dozen people in the lobby. This is a red flag. No company that small should be interviewing that many people on a daily basis.

My curiosity sufficiently aroused, I asked a passing interviewer what his company did, and he responded with a scripted explanation of the services they provide to companies. I heard the words "marketing," "solutions," and "sales." He then ended with some energetic fanboy disclaimer of "We have tons of fun." or something like that. My suspicions were confirmed: This is a pyramid scheme.

In truth, life is a pyramid scheme, especially in a capitalist country, but Multi-Level Marketing is a scourge on the name of Adam Smith's legacy. The high turnover and dubious legality mean MLM firms must walk a fine line between business-as-usual and secrecy. All their employees are independent contractors, and temp space is crucial in case a former employee rats you out to regulatory entity and you need a new business filing and address.

I'm watching all these recruits come in, bright-eyed and bushy-tailed, dressed in suits and carrying executive note pads...no doubt the ones who made a 3.0 in college and possess few marketable skills other than "works well with others" and "excellent communicator." They come in all age ranges, some early graduates, others middle-aged guys looking for something new and exciting.

They're all so nervous, and it disgusts me to hear the interviewers leading them down this hall asking if they've prepared for the interview. I'm sure the interview itself would make me vomit or throw something - some fatuous 30something call-center goon grilling a young man on his third job in a year about his life goals and how he can fit into the company's mission of force-selling AT&T Uverse subscriptions to bored housewives and impoverished minorities.

The other day I caught a cute girl coming out of one of these interviews. I followed her into the lobby on my way to the restroom and asked her how her interview went. She said it went well. I asked her if it was Multi-Level. She stopped, looked at me, fondled her notepad, and said sheepishly "Yes." I said "Ok, just checking."

I should've said "Be careful," or "Make sure you know what you're getting yourself into," but I didn't want to sound patronizing, I just wanted to raise an idea in her mind. I hope it helped, because today I've already seen a few interviewees walking down my hall and I don't want to see her back here as an employee.

I feel sorry for them, but they have to learn about getting screwed over, and at least they'll get paid a little bit of money to learn the hard way.
